Comprehensive Summary
The direct reductive coupling of carbonyl compounds with propargyl halides is a powerful and reliable tool in the synthesis of
α-allenols. However, stoichiometric metal reductants, harsh reaction conditions and a variety of additional additives are required in
the traditional strategies. Additionally, the reactivity and regioselectivity control remains an elusive challenge. Herein, we developed
the Ti-catalyzed regioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes and racemic propargyl bromides to rapidly access a
wide range of α-allenols. This method proceed efficiently in a reductive radical-polar crossover manner featuring mild conditions, ex-
cellent regioselectivity control, broad substrate scope, and eco-friendliness. Preliminary mechanistic studies support the radical-in-
volved catalytic cycle. And the DFT calculations demonstrate that the regioselectivity is determined by the Zimmerman-Traxler-type
transition states.
Background and Originality Content
α-Allenols not only bear the π-activated hydroxyl unit showing
an extra reactivity toward substitutions or eliminations, but also
have allene group that can promote cycloaddition, electropholic
addition, or metal-catalyzed coupling reaction.<sup>[1-4]</sup> The presence of
both the functional groups endows the unique value of allenols in
the synthesis of many bioactive molecules, natural products and
pharmaceutical molecules (Figure 1a).<sup>[4-6]</sup> The conventional ap-
proaches to the synthesis of α-allenols start from alkynes or acti-
vated allenes through homologation of propargylic alcohols or
addition with carbonyl compounds (Figure 1b).<sup>[1,3]</sup> Many excellent
reports have been achieved by Ma,<sup>[7]</sup> Feng,<sup>[8]</sup> List<sup>[9]</sup> and other
groups<sup>[10-16]</sup> with transition-metal catalysts. However, these reac-
tions primarily focus on ionic pathway via a two-electron transfer.
In sharp contrast, radical chemistry could endow the efficient
construction of allenols stereoselectively under mild condition but
remains limited explored.<sup>[4,17-18]</sup> Therefore, further exploration of
new reaction patterns involving radicals that enable the synthesis
of allenols in an efficient, selective, straightforward and
eco-friendly manner is highly desired.

Nowadays, the radical-polar crossover has emerged as a po-
tent strategy in organic chemistry.<sup>[18-23]</sup> With this strategy, the
radical intermediate could been transformed into an electrophile
or nucleophile via single-electron transfer (SET). Notably, it pro-
vides a potential solution for the synthesis of allenes. While the
regioselectivity control remains an elusive challenge owing to the
rearrangement between propargylic radicals and allenyl radi-
cals.<sup>[4,17-18,24]</sup> Many reports about the synthesis of allenes were
disclosed by the groups of Liu,<sup>[25]</sup> Ma,<sup>[26]</sup> Wang,<sup>[27]</sup> Bao,<sup>[28-29]</sup> and
others<sup>[30-32]</sup> independently through the cross-coupling of the pre-
formed nucleophile-metal species with allenyl radicals (Figure 1c,
top). However, the transition metal-catalyzed allenylation of al-
dehydes to access α-allenols via reductive radical-polar crossover
reaction remains less explored. Although several elegant methods
have been developed by Nakada,<sup>[33]</sup> Yamamoto,<sup>[34]</sup> Guiry,<sup>[35]</sup>
Oltra,<sup>[36]</sup> and Wang<sup>[4]</sup> groups via Cr/Ti-catalyzed reductive coupling
of propargyl halides and carbonyl compounds to rapidly afford
various valuable allenols (Figure 1c, bottom), stoichiometric metal
reductants and a variety of additional additives are required in
this reaction. In comparison, photoredox catalysis has the ad-
vantage of mild condition, easy regulation, and environmental
friendliness and plays an indispensable role in the radical synthe-
sis as well.<sup>[37-38]</sup> In 2022, Wang group<sup>[17]</sup> described the elegant
photoredox/Cr co-catalyzed enantioselective synthesis of α-alle-
nols through a radical-involved redox-neutral pathway. And to the
best of our knowledge, it’s also the only report on the synthesis of
α-allenols through metallaphotoredox. Thus, it is necessary to
develop alternative photoredox catalysis to enrich the diversity of
the reaction.
Titanium is one of the most abundant inexpensive transition
metals and highly attractive for the development of novel catalytic
radical reaction because the metal frequently and efficiently un-
dergoes facile one-electron oxidation state changes.<sup>[39-40]</sup> Moreo-
ver, based on the previous observations,<sup>[41-43]</sup> Cp<sub>2</sub>Ti<sup>III</sup>Cl as a good
one-electron reductant can be prepared in situ from the higher
valent

In addition, the limited oxidizing power of Ti<sup>IV</sup>
radical intermediates, which may impede the cyclic regeneration
of titanium catalyst, can be overcome by photoredox cataly-
sis.<sup>[44-45]</sup> Herein, we describe the photoredox and titanium
co-catalyzed regioselective coupling of aldehydes with propargyl
bromides via reductive radical-polar crossover (Figure 1d). Distinct
from the previous work,<sup>[41,46]</sup> we envisioned that the allenylation
instead of propargylation could proceed through precise control
over reaction parameters. This methodology not only obviates the
need of stoichiometric metal reductants, or additional additives,
but also features mild conditions, good functional group compati-
bility, and broad substrate scope.
Results and Discussion
We commenced the allenylation reaction with phenylpropyl
aldehyde (1a) and (3-bromoprop-1-yn-1-yl)benzene (2a) as the
model substrates (Table 1). After detailed investigation of an array
of reaction parameters, we determined that the merger of
Cp TiCl co-catalysis with 4CzIPN could achieve the regioselective
allenylation reaction in good yield under visible-light irradiation
(Table 1, entry 1). The reaction could also provide the desired
product in CH<sub>3</sub>CN, DCM, or 1,4-dioxane with a decrease in yield
(Table 1, entries 2, 5—6). While trace yield was achieved when
DCE, toluene, DMF, or DMSO was used as the solvent (Table 1,
entries 3—4, 7—8). When decreasing the concentration from 0.1
mol/L to 0.05 mol/L, the yield decreased from 60% to 38% (Table
1, entry 9). And the reaction was also performed well when the
concentration was increased from 0.1 mol/L to 0.3 mol/L (Table 1,
entries 10—11). The allenylation product was also affected when
the amount of 2a, HE, or Cp TiCl was changed (Table 1, entries
12—17). It is noteworthy that the product of 3a could be obtained
in the yield of 69%, if 20 mol% Cp TiCl was used (Table 1, entry
17). The photocatalysts Ir-2 or Ir-3 also led to the product but with
an erosion in yield (Table 1, entries 19—20). The satisfying result
was achieved when 7 mol% Ir-1 and 20 mol% Cp<sub>2</sub>TiCl<sub>2</sub> were per-
formed (Table 1, entry 18, 21—22). And the yield was basically
unchanged when Ir-1 was further increased (Table 1, entry 23).
Control experiments disclosed that Cp<sub>2</sub>TiCl<sub>2</sub>, photocatalyst, HE,
and light are indispensable for this allenylation reaction (Table 1,
entries 24—27).
Based on the optimal conditions, we explored the synthetic
scope of aldehyde firstly. It is pleasing that a broad array of ali-
phatic and aromatic aldehydes can proceed smoothly to afford
the α-allenols in moderate to good yields (Figure 2, 3a—3x). To
our delight, apart from the tethered aldehydes (3a—3f), the cyclic
aldehydes (3g—3j) could also react well with (3-bromoprop-1-yn-
1-yl)benzene. And the presence of heteroatoms has no effect on
the process of allenylation (3i—3j). In addition, various functional
groups are compatible under the mild conditions, including CF<sub>3</sub>

Furthermore, the scope of the propargyl bromides was also
investigated (Figure 3, 4a—4r). Various propargyl bromides with
different terminal substituents reacted efficiently with the alde-
hyde to provide the desired α-allenols in the yield of 45%—87%

ponent could afford the desired propargylation products (4n—4r).
According to previous reports,<sup>[46]</sup> the type of products is con-
trolled by the different energy barriers in transition states relative
to the reaction of the propargyl and allenyl titanium(IV) precur-
sors with carbonyls. Additionally, no allenylation product or pro-
pargylation product could be obtained when more sterically hin-
dered (3-bromohex-1-yn-1-yl)benzene was used as the substrate.

optimized condition. And the single electron reduction of propar-

hydrogen transfer reaction. DFT calculations suggest that regiose-
lectivity is determined by the Zimmerman−Traxler-type transition
states.<sup>[30]</sup> And the lower Gibbs free energy of the intermediates of

Conclusions
In this study, we have demonstrated a novel reductive radi-
cal-polar crossover coupling reaction of aldehydes with propargyl
bromides through dual photoredox and titanium catalysis. This
eco-friendly method exhibits good substrate scope and excep-
tional functional group compatibility, providing facile access to
valuable α-allenols from readily available starting material. Mean-
while, the super-stoichiometric metal reductants and external
additives are not required. The development of new catalytic sys-
tems for allenols synthesis based on dual photoredox and titani-
um catalysis is underway in our group.
Experimental
An oven-dried Schlenk tube equipped with an stirring bar was
charged under nitrogen gas with the corresponding propargyl
bromides (2, 2.0 equiv.), aldehyde (1, 0.2 mmol), Ir-1 (10 mol%),
Hantzsch ester (HE, 2.0 equiv.),
\mathsf { c p } _ { 2 } \mathsf { T i C l } _ { 2 }
(20 mol%), and THF (0.1
mol/L, 2.0 mL). The reaction mixture was then degassed by
freeze-pump-thaw for three times, then the vessel was back-filled
with nitrogen gas. The substrate was added after being degassed
when it’s a liquid. Subsequently, the reaction was stirred at room
temperature under blue LEDs irradiation (10 W, 455 nm) for 2 h.
The reaction solution was concentrated in vacuo and then purified
by column chromatography on silica gel (pentane/EtOAc) to afford
the corresponding compounds.
